food.text: Hallstatt in Austria is known for salt production that dates back to prehistoric times. During the Bronze Age, salt production there became a day-to-day commercial activity, and salt was produced in large quantities.
Farmers of the Urnfield culture in Central Europe grew wheat and barley, together with pulses and the horse bean. This late Bronze Age culture lasted from about 1300 to 750 BC.

Along the Roman-era Amber Road, which ran from the Baltic coast through the land of the Boii to Aquileia, traders carried more than amber. Honey and wax were exported to the Romans, along with animal fur and skin, in exchange for Roman glass, brass, gold and metals such as tin and copper.
The Hallstatt salt works were highly organized, and specialist workers supported the mining operations. The wealth this trade generated is on display in the prehistoric cemeteries at Hallstatt.
The Hallstatt culture was based on farming and takes its name from Hallstatt, a lakeside village with a rich salt mine. Some 1,300 burials are known there, many with fine artifacts.
Urnfield farmers used poppy seeds for oil or as a drug. Flax seems to have been of reduced importance, maybe because mainly wool was used for clothes.

Major activity at the Hallstatt salt site appears to have finished about 500 BC, for reasons that are unclear. Many Hallstatt graves were robbed, probably at this time, as there was widespread disruption throughout the western Hallstatt zone. By then the salt workings had become very deep.

art.text: Some of the most spectacular Bronze Age finds from central Europe are golden hats, and their finds are centred on Germany. The region was also the heartland of the 'central' form of the Urnfield culture, and of the Hallstatt culture that followed it.

The Hallstatt culture grew out of the Urnfield culture and was the predominant culture of Western and Central Europe from the 12th to 8th centuries BC and into the early Iron Age. It was followed by the La Tène culture, which lasted from the 5th to the 1st centuries BC.

Roman remains from around 100 to 150 AD can still be seen along the limes, the border defence system that marked the edge of the Roman Empire in what is now Germany. Besides forts and military camps, the Romans also built thermae, bridges and amphitheatres there.

Celtic cultural centres developed in central Europe from about 1200 BC until 700 BC. One of them, the Heuneburg, is described as the oldest city north of the Alps. It became an important Iron Age centre and kept up trade routes to the Mediterranean.

The people in central and southern Germany who adopted the Urnfield and Hallstatt cultural traits are regarded as Celts. How, and even whether, the Celts are related to the Urnfield culture remains disputed.

The Romans regarded glassblowing as having originated in Syria in the 1st century BC. By the 3rd century, Egypt and the Rhineland had become noted for their fine glass. The Rhineland was thus a centre of luxury craftsmanship within the Roman world.

war.text: Between 8 and 11 September 9 CE, an alliance of Germanic peoples ambushed three Roman legions and their auxiliaries led by Publius Quinctilius Varus, possibly near modern Kalkriese. The Germanic warriors stormed the field and slaughtered the disintegrating Roman forces. Roman casualties have been estimated at 15,000 to 20,000 dead, Varus committed suicide, and many officers were said to have fallen on their swords. Roman historians called it the Varian Disaster.

The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest is considered one of the most important defeats in Roman history. It brought the triumphant period of expansion under Augustus to an abrupt end. It also dissuaded the Romans from pursuing the conquest of Germania.

The Germanic alliance was led by Arminius, a Germanic chieftain who was also an officer of Varus's auxilia. He had received Roman citizenship and a Roman military education. This let him deceive the Romans methodically and anticipate their tactical responses.

After the defeat, Tiberius and Germanicus commanded retaliatory campaigns that enjoyed success. Germanicus burned the city of Mattium to the ground, and his legions inflicted huge casualties on the Germanic armies. He also devastated the land of the Marsi, and when his troops visited the first battle site, Tacitus says they found heaps of bleached bones and severed skulls nailed to trees. Even so, the Rhine became the border between the Roman Empire and the rest of Germania, with Germania Superior and Germania Inferior established in northeast Roman Gaul while territories beyond the Rhine remained independent.

Augustus sought to tame the Germanic tribes and made his stepson Drusus governor of Gaul. Drusus campaigned against the Germans from 11 to 9 BCE and won a series of victories despite considerable obstacles. He died in a riding accident in 9 BCE.

Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus suppressed a number of local uprisings and then crossed the Elbe river. He was the first and last Roman general to do so. Romans of the time felt secure about Germany, reassured by thriving cross-border trade and relative peace.

In 11 BCE the Cherusci trapped Drusus' army in unfavourable terrain, and the Romans escaped only with great difficulty. McNally argues Arminius drew a lesson from this: the Romans could be defeated, but only where their tactical flexibility and discipline could not be brought to bear.

Drusus defeated the Cherusci in 8 BCE, and as a result Arminius was made a hostage. McNally suggests this victory would have been unforgettable to him. It is one of two events said to have shaped his view of the Romans.

literature.text: In 1812 a farmer, Jurij Slaček, found 26 bronze helmets stacked inside each other in a cache near Negau while clearing land, in what is now Slovenia. He broke one helmet during a test and sold the other 25 to a coppersmith, Johann Denzl. Twenty-three helmets survive, dating to about 450 BC to 350 BC, and two of the missing ones are thought to have been melted down by Denzl. One survivor, Negau B, carries an inscription in a northern Etruscan alphabet.

Around 98 AD the Roman historian Tacitus wrote the Germania, originally titled On the Origin and Situation of the Germans. It is an ethnographic work on the Germanic peoples living outside the Roman Empire. It follows a tradition of ethnography that runs from Herodotus to Julius Caesar.

About 350 inscriptions in the Elder Futhark script are known, dating from the 2nd to the 8th centuries AD. Around 81 are Continental or South Germanic, including German and Gothic. The South Germanic tradition shows a preference for fibulae as the objects that carry inscriptions.

The Negau B inscription runs right to left. Tom Markey read it in 2001 as Hariχasti teiva, 'Harigast the priest'. Another helmet from the site bears several names, mostly Celtic, followed by religious titles, which supports that reading. Markey reads the four inscriptions on the helmet called Negau A as including Dubni banuabi, 'of Dubnos the pig-slayer', and sirago turbi, 'astral priest of the troop'.

The first 27 chapters of Tacitus' Germania describe the lands, laws and customs of the various tribes. Later chapters take particular tribes in turn, starting with those closest to the Roman empire. The book ends with peoples on the shores of the Baltic Sea, such as the Fenni.

The Rhaetic alphabet of Bolzano is often proposed as the origin of the runes. Only five Elder Futhark runes have no counterpart in it. Scandinavian scholars tend to favor derivation from the Latin alphabet itself instead.
Some scholars once saw the Negau B inscription as an early form of runic writing. It is now accepted that the script is North Etruscan proper and came before the Runic alphabet was formed.

The Negau B inscription may be the earliest attestation of Grimm's law, the First Germanic Sound Shift. If teiva is a Germanic cousin of Latin deus, 'god', it shows the shift from d to t. Jeremy J. Smith, however, argues there are major problems with treating the helmet as conclusive evidence.

The Germania was one of the minor works of Tacitus and was not widely cited or used before the Renaissance. In antiquity, Lucian appears to have imitated a sentence from it. The work was largely forgotten during the Middle Ages.

A silver-plated copper disk from a sword-belt, found at Liebenau in Lower Saxony, carries an early 5th-century runic inscription, possibly reading rauzwih. It is mostly illegible, but is classed as the earliest known South Germanic inscription.
A silver neck ring found near Aalen has the word noru inscribed in runes on its inner edge. It is one of several legible and partly interpretable inscriptions from the first half of the 5th century.

The Meldorf inscription of 50 AD may count as proto-runic use of the Latin alphabet by Germanic speakers. It is one of the clues scholars use to work out how the first runic alphabet was created, which is generally dated to roughly the 1st century.

politics.text: Maroboduus, born into a noble Marcomanni family, spent part of his youth in Rome, then returned to his people around 9 BC as their king. To escape Roman expansion, he led them into Bohemia and organized a confederation of neighboring Germanic tribes. He is the earliest recorded ruler of the territory of the modern Czech Republic.

In 9 AD, Arminius, a Germanic chieftain who had received Roman citizenship and a Roman military education, ambushed three Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus. The Germanic warriors stormed the field and slaughtered the disintegrating Roman forces; Roman casualties have been estimated at 15,000–20,000 dead, and Varus committed suicide. The defeat brought Augustus's period of expansion to an abrupt end and dissuaded Rome from pursuing the conquest of Germania.

The Marcomannic Wars lasted from about 166 until 180 CE and pitted Rome against the Marcomanni, the Quadi and the Sarmatian Iazyges along the Danube. They came after troops returning from the Parthian war brought home the Antonine Plague, which would eventually kill an estimated 7 to 8 million people. The Marcomanni defeated a Roman force of 20,000 near Carnuntum, ravaged Noricum, destroyed Oderzo and besieged Aquileia, the first hostile incursion into Italy since 101 BC. The wars occupied most of Marcus Aurelius's reign, and he began writing his Meditations during these campaigns.

Noricum was a kingdom or federation of tribes covering most of modern Austria and part of Slovenia. Its tribes gradually united from 200 BC, and it became a key ally of Rome by supplying high-quality weapons and tools in exchange for military protection. It was incorporated into the Roman Empire in 16 BC.

In 6 AD Augustus planned to destroy Maroboduus's kingdom, which he considered too dangerous for Rome. Tiberius commanded 12 legions against the Marcomanni, but a revolt in Illyria forced him to make a treaty and recognize Maroboduus as king.

Arminius, born about 18 or 17 BC, was a prince of the Cherusci who learned Latin and served in the Roman military. When he plotted to unite the Germanic tribes against Rome, the task proved difficult, because the tribes were strongly independent and many were traditional enemies of each other.

Arminius sent the head of Varus to Maroboduus, but the Marcomannic king sent it on to Augustus. In 17 AD war broke out between the two rulers, and their rivalry prevented a concerted attack on Roman territory across the Rhine and the Danube.

After Catualda defeated Maroboduus, the deposed king fled to Italy. Tiberius detained him for 18 years in Ravenna, where he died in 37 AD. Catualda was in turn defeated by the Hermunduri Vibilius, after which the Quadian Vannius ruled until Vibilius deposed him too, letting his nephews Vangio and Sido rule as Roman client kings.

Tiberius, who succeeded Augustus in AD 14, judged Germania a far less developed land with few villages and only a small food surplus. Conquering it would have required a commitment too burdensome for imperial finances and military force. The Rhine became the border.

In 171 AD, Marcus Aurelius ran the Danubian campaign from a headquarters at Carnuntum, between present-day Vienna and Bratislava. The Quadi agreed to leave their coalition and returned 13,000 prisoners of war, but by 173 AD they had rebelled and expelled their Roman-approved king Furtius, replacing him with Ariogaisos.

Around 16 BC, Publius Silius Nerva completed the conquest of the eastern Alps after the Pannonians and Norics invaded Istria. He occupied southern Noricum and made the kingdom of northern Noricum a kind of vassal state.

politics.text: Gallienus, who reigned 253 to 268 AD, settled the Marcomanni within the Roman province of Pannonia Superior, south of the Danube. He also took Pipa (or Pipara), the daughter of the Marcomanni king Attalus, as a concubine.

philosophy.text: Christianity reached the area of modern Germany by 300 AD, while parts of it still belonged to the Roman Empire. Later, from the fifth century onwards, the Franks and other Germanic tribes converted as well.

Pagan Roman temples already stood in the Roman lands of Germany before Christian buildings appeared. One early Christian structure was the Aula Palatina in Trier, completed during the reign of Emperor Constantine I (306–337).

Judaism also has deep roots in the region. Jewish communities in German-speaking regions go back to the fourth century, the same period in which Christianity began to flourish in the Roman provinces there.

In the Roman provinces of Raetia, Germania Superior and Germania Inferior, early Christianity was introduced and began to flourish after the fourth century. Trier, home of the Aula Palatina, was then the capital of the province Gallia Belgica.

culture.text: The Urnfield culture takes its name from the custom of cremating the dead and placing their ashes in urns, which were then buried in fields. It was a late Bronze Age culture of Central Europe, dated to about 1300 to 750 BC.

According to the traditional theory, the proto-Celtic language arose in the late Bronze Age Urnfield culture of central Europe, named after grave sites in southern Germany. That culture flourished from around 1200 BC. Celtic culture is then thought to have spread westward and southward from these areas.

The La Tène culture flourished from about 450 BC until the Roman conquest in the 1st century BC, succeeding the Hallstatt culture without any definite cultural break. Its territory included southern Germany, Austria, Switzerland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovenia.

Ancient Germanic paganism was a polytheistic religion practised in prehistoric Germany and in Roman territories of Germania by the first century AD. Its pantheon included Donar/Thunar, Wuotan/Wodan, Frouwa/Frua and Balder/Phol/Baldag.

The spread of iron-working led to the Hallstatt culture developing out of the Urnfield culture in a wide region north of the Alps. It lasted from about 800 to 500 BC. It is named for the rich grave finds in Hallstatt, Austria.

Christianity was introduced to the area of modern Germany by 300 AD, while parts of it belonged to the Roman Empire. In the provinces of Raetia, Germania Superior and Germania Inferior, it began to flourish after the fourth century, following earlier pagan Roman temples.
Jewish communities in German-speaking regions go back to the fourth century, the same period in which early Christianity began to flourish in the Roman provinces there.

The La Tène culture developed under considerable Mediterranean influence from the Greeks, the Etruscans and the Golasecca culture. Even so, its artistic style did not depend on those Mediterranean influences.

By about 400 BCE, evidence for Mediterranean trade becomes sparse, possibly because expanding Celtic populations began to migrate south and west, coming into violent conflict with the established populations, including the Etruscans and Romans. Settled life in much of the La Tène homelands also seems to have become much more unstable and prone to wars.
Celtic paganism and later Gallo-Roman syntheses were practised in the western and southern parts of modern Germany. This set them apart from the Germanic paganism found elsewhere in the region.

Christian buildings soon appeared in Roman Germany, such as the Aula Palatina in Trier. Trier was then the capital of the Roman province Gallia Belgica. The building was completed during the reign of Emperor Constantine I (306–337).
Frey (2004) notes that in the 5th century, burial customs in the Celtic world were not uniform; localised groups had their own beliefs, which also gave rise to distinct artistic expressions.
